hero_lede: Spoken language models are evaluated by a fast-growing, fast-fragmenting pile of benchmarks. This site indexes them in one place — what each one actually measures, how they group by capability, when each appeared on arXiv, and how models score where scores have been published. It is rebuilt every day from a fresh crawl of new arXiv postings.
overview: A spoken LLM here means a model that takes speech in and/or produces speech out and is meant to be general-purpose. That definition is doing real work: it is what separates this field from the decades of speech research that preceded it. A system that only transcribes, or only synthesises, is not in scope no matter how good it is — the interesting question about a spoken LLM is whether it can do many things it was never specifically trained for.

That shift broke evaluation. When a model did one task, you measured that task: word error rate, or a mean opinion score. When a model claims to do everything, there is no single number, and the community has responded by building benchmarks at a rate that is now genuinely hard to follow — dozens per year, scattered across speech venues, NLP venues, and arXiv preprints that never reach a venue at all.
scope_note: A benchmark is included if the system under test is a general-purpose speech or audio language model. Benchmarks that only measure transcription accuracy (ASR) or only synthesis quality (TTS) are excluded, even when spoken LLMs are used to produce the output. Audio-understanding benchmarks covering sounds, scenes and music are included when the model under test is a general audio-language model rather than a dedicated classifier.
overview_more: Two surveys anchor the pre-2025 picture and are cited throughout: Yang, Ho & Lee, Towards Holistic Evaluation of Large Audio-Language Models (EMNLP 2025), and Arora et al., On The Landscape of Spoken Language Models (TMLR 2025). Both were read end to end to seed this catalogue. Everything dated 2025 onwards was collected independently, by a systematic arXiv API sweep rather than by recall, and then verified against each paper.

The catalogue is deliberately opinionated about provenance. Every arXiv identifier here was read off the arXiv API or the paper's own abstract page. Every number in the comparison tables carries a citation back to the source it was copied from. Where a date, an identifier or a score could not be verified, the field is left empty rather than filled in — an empty cell is information, a plausible-looking wrong one is not.
table_caveat: These tables aggregate published numbers; nothing here was re-run. Scores for the same model on the same benchmark can differ between sources because the prompt, the decoding settings, the judge model, the audio rendering of text prompts, and the model checkpoint all vary — and many benchmarks changed between versions. Read a column as "what this benchmark's authors, or this model's authors, reported", not as a controlled head-to-head. Rows are sorted by how many of the category's benchmarks a model has scores for, so the most-evaluated models sit at the top. A blank cell means not reported, never zero.
paper_blurb: Alongside the catalogue there is a written survey of the field, focused on the 2025-onwards wave: what the new benchmarks measure that the older ones did not, where the field has converged, where it has duplicated itself, and what still has no benchmark at all.
It is written against this catalogue, so every count in it can be checked against the data files in the repository, and every benchmark it names carries the arXiv identifier recorded here.

contribute: This catalogue will be wrong somewhere. Benchmarks get renamed, papers get revised, scores get corrected, and a systematic sweep still misses things — especially work that does not use the word "benchmark" in its abstract, and work published outside English-language venues.

If you find an error, or your benchmark is missing, or a number is out of date, please write. Corrections are checked against the original paper and applied, and every edit is listed in the changelog below.
contribute_note: Useful things to include: the arXiv identifier or paper link, which capability the benchmark targets, and — for a score correction — which table in which paper the correct number comes from. Corrections that cannot be traced to a published source will not be applied, and you will get a reply saying so. Mail is read once a day.
disclosure: How this site is maintained — and what it is not. This atlas is built and maintained by an AI agent (Claude Fable 5), not by a human editor: it exists because Hung-yi Lee casually prompted the agent and wanted to see what AI agents can do. No human has verified its content, and it is not an official publication of ISCA or any other body. The daily arXiv crawl is a plain script with no model in the loop, so it cannot invent papers; the catalogue entries, the classification and the overview paper are AI-written and AI-checked against the source papers, with every identifier and every number traced to where it came from. That process is careful, not infallible — treat the site as a well-sourced index to read the primary papers from, never as a citable authority. It is an independent project and speaks for no institution or organisation; since 31 August 2026 it is part of the SCOOT 2.0 collection of speech-communication references — itself unofficial and equally unverified. Corrections are genuinely welcome and are what keep it honest.
geo_intro: For the benchmarks whose papers print author affiliations, those affiliations were read from the paper itself and confirmed by an independent second read; for the models in the tables, the releasing organisation was taken from the model’s own paper, report or model card. Coverage is stated below, not assumed. Institutions sit on the map at the site the paper names when it names one, otherwise at the organisation’s main campus or headquarters; countries are shaded by their total. Switch between counting every author’s institution, only the lead institution, or the builders of the models.
geo_method:
Source. For each benchmark the affiliations were read off the paper: the author block of the arXiv HTML rendering, or the first page of the PDF where the HTML omits affiliations. At that step city and country were recorded only when printed; where a paper prints no affiliation but does print e-mail addresses, the organisation was taken from the domain and marked as such. An independent second pass then re-read every header and tried to refute the first reading — a wrong superscript mapping, a department recorded as the organisation, a footnote mistaken for an affiliation. A record is counted only when that second read confirmed it, or replaced it with a correction that quotes the text; records the checker could not confirm are kept in the data files but excluded from the attribution statistics (they appear only in the coverage counts above). For models, the builder is the organisation named on the model’s own paper, technical report, model card or the vendor’s official model page, and a record is counted only with that evidence link on file (a model whose only evidence is a third party’s paper is kept on file but not counted); cascades assembled from third-party parts (an ASR model feeding a text LLM) are not attributed by design.

Canonical names and places. Raw affiliation strings were then mapped to one organisation each: the whole university (departments, schools and joint labs are kept as units; separate campuses stay separate), the parent company (Tencent AI Lab and WeChat AI are both Tencent; Google DeepMind is Google; FAIR is Meta), or the member institute for umbrella bodies such as the Chinese Academy of Sciences. This is the one step that uses world knowledge — resolving that NTU means Nanyang Technological University when the paper says Singapore and National Taiwan University when it says Taipei — and every distinct raw string keeps one resolved country, city and confidence level in institutions.json (a string that means different sites in different papers keeps only one). Two organisations that share an English name are kept apart only when they sit in different countries. Coordinates are city centres: the site named on the paper when one is named (Microsoft Research Asia sits in Beijing, not Redmond), otherwise the organisation’s main campus or headquarters, which the map tooltip says. Each coordinate was checked against its country’s bounding box where one exists (latitude only for countries that straddle the antimeridian) — a coarse check that catches a wrong country, not a wrong city — and every organisation city was independently geocoded with OpenStreetMap and compared (394 matched within 60 km, 9 the geocoder could not resolve, 4 same-name clashes reviewed by hand); cities printed on papers were geocoded the same way. A second model (Codex) reviewed the counting policy, the prose, the canonical names, countries and coordinates, and spot-checked records against the papers before publication; its corrections are applied.

Counting. Whole counts, not fractional. Any author: a benchmark counts once for each distinct organisation on its paper, and once for each country those organisations’ sites sit in. Lead: at most one organisation per benchmark — the first-listed affiliation of the first author (a paper whose first author lists no organisation has no lead) — so the lead-based percentages partition. A model counts once for each releasing organisation. The year chart and the region groups (China incl. Hong Kong and Macau; Europe incl. the UK, Switzerland and Ukraine, but not Russia or Turkey) use the lead institution’s country; the full mapping is under the chart.

Limits. Affiliations are what was printed at submission; people move. First-page text extraction is imperfect, especially for glued tokens and multi-column layouts, so some records are marked partial. Organisation sizes are not normalised: Tencent counted once is the same as a single-lab university counted once, and a joint lab printed as five parent organisations credits all five. Two different organisations that happen to share an English name would be merged, and a spelling variant that the merge step missed would be split. The daily crawl that adds benchmarks does not add their affiliations automatically; new entries show as not yet attributed on their record and in the coverage box until the next pass.
